introduction.summary: Gravitation is the universal attractive interaction between masses. It explains falling bodies, the Moon’s motion, planetary motion and artificial satellites.
learning_objectives: Understand gravitation as a universal attractive interaction between masses.
Understand the historical development from early astronomical models to Newton's law.
Recognise the role of gravitation in planetary, lunar and satellite motion.

explanation: Gravitation is the universal attractive interaction between any two bodies having mass.
Every mass attracts every other mass. The effect is small for ordinary objects but becomes dominant for planets, stars, moons and satellites.
Falling objects, the Moon's motion around Earth, planetary motion around the Sun, artificial satellites and many astronomical phenomena are explained using gravitation.
Gravity is the gravitational attraction experienced near a celestial body such as Earth.
Gravitational force is always attractive and acts along the line joining the centres of the interacting bodies.

worked_example.title: Why an object falls
worked_example.problem: A body released near Earth accelerates downward. Which interaction causes this acceleration?
worked_example.solution: Earth attracts the body gravitationally; the resulting force is F=GMm/R² and therefore produces acceleration g.

worked_example.title: Mass versus gravity
worked_example.problem: If the same object is taken from Earth to Moon, what changes?
worked_example.solution: Its mass remains the same, while its weight changes because local g is different.

worked_example.title: Universal nature
worked_example.problem: Does gravitation act only on planets?
worked_example.solution: No. Every mass attracts every other mass; planets are simply large systems where the effect is obvious.

visualization.title: From falling object to satellite
visualization.purpose: Connect everyday falling motion with celestial motion.
visualization.note: Interactive component not yet built. Controls and outputs below define exactly what the next AI-generated visualizer for this topic should let the student manipulate and see.

key_points: The force acts along the line joining the centres.
Gravity near a celestial body is the gravitational attraction experienced there.
The same basic law explains terrestrial and celestial gravitational phenomena.
common_mistakes: Confusing gravitational force with g.
Thinking gravitation acts only between planets.
neet_tips: Start every gravitation problem by identifying the two masses and centre-to-centre distance.

introduction.summary: Kepler’s laws describe planetary motion and provide the observational foundation connecting orbital geometry, speed and period.

subsections.title: First Law — Law of Orbits
subsections.content: Every planet moves in an elliptical orbit with the Sun situated at one focus of the ellipse.
points: The circle is a special case of an ellipse.
Closest point to the Sun is perihelion.
The semi-major axis is half the major axis.

subsections.title: Second Law — Law of Areas
subsections.content: The line joining a planet and the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal intervals of time.
points: A planet moves faster near perihelion.
A planet moves slower near aphelion.
The law is related to conservation of angular momentum.

subsections.title: Third Law — Law of Periods
subsections.content: The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis.

formulae.label: Third Law — Law of Periods
formulae.formula: T^2/a^3 = constant for bodies orbiting the same central mass

worked_example.title: Perihelion speed
worked_example.problem: A planet is closer to the Sun at perihelion. Is its speed larger or smaller than at aphelion?
worked_example.solution: By Kepler’s second law, equal areas are swept in equal times, so the planet moves faster when it is closer.

worked_example.title: Period scaling
worked_example.problem: If the orbital size changes from a to 2a around the same Sun, how does T change?

worked_example.title: Areal velocity
worked_example.problem: What remains constant for a planet according to Kepler’s second law?
worked_example.solution: The area swept per unit time by the Sun–planet line remains constant.

visualization.title: Kepler's Laws — Interactive Visualization
visualization.description: Switch between the 1st, 2nd and 3rd laws. The 2nd-law view animates a planet on an elliptical orbit and shades two equal swept areas (near and far from the Sun) so students see directly why the planet speeds up near perihelion.

key_points: First law: ellipse with Sun at one focus.
Second law: equal areas in equal times.
Third law: T²∝a³ for bodies orbiting the same central mass.
common_mistakes: Putting the Sun at the centre of the ellipse instead of a focus.
Using radius instead of semi-major axis for a general ellipse.
neet_tips: For perihelion/aphelion speed questions, think angular momentum/areal velocity first.

introduction.summary: Newton’s universal law gives the magnitude and direction of gravitational attraction between masses.

explanation: Two masses attract each other with force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres.

explanation.heading: Properties
points: Force acts along the line joining the masses.
Forces on the two masses are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
Force decreases as inverse square of separation.
The law applies to point masses and to spherically symmetric bodies using centre-to-centre distance.

worked_example.title: Distance scaling
worked_example.problem: If separation doubles while masses stay fixed, what happens to F?
worked_example.solution: F∝1/r², so F′=F/4.

worked_example.title: Mass scaling
worked_example.problem: If both masses are doubled, what happens to F?
worked_example.solution: F∝m1m2, so F′=4F.

worked_example.title: Superposition
worked_example.problem: Several masses act on a test mass. How is net force found?
worked_example.solution: Add the gravitational force vectors from each source: F⃗net=ΣF⃗i.

visualization.title: Change Mass and Distance
visualization.purpose: Show direct mass dependence and inverse-square distance dependence.
visualization.note: Interactive component not yet built. Controls and outputs below define exactly what the next AI-generated visualizer for this topic should let the student manipulate and see.

key_points: Equal and opposite forces act on the two interacting bodies.
For spherically symmetric bodies outside the body, centre-to-centre distance is used.
common_mistakes: Using surface-to-surface distance instead of centre-to-centre distance.
Adding scalar magnitudes when force directions differ.
neet_tips: For ratios, write F∝m1m2/r² before substituting numbers.

introduction.summary: G is the universal constant that sets the strength scale of Newtonian gravitation.

explanation: G is the universal gravitational constant.
G is approximately 6.67 × 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2.
G is universal; g is location-dependent.

worked_example.title: Dimensions
worked_example.problem: Find dimensions of G.
worked_example.solution: G=Fr²/m². Since [F]=MLT^-2, [G]=M^-1L³T^-2.

worked_example.title: Unit
worked_example.problem: What is the SI unit of G?
worked_example.solution: From G=Fr²/m1m2, the unit is N m² kg^-2.

worked_example.title: G versus g
worked_example.problem: Does G change from Earth to Moon?
worked_example.solution: G is universal; g is location-dependent.

visualization.title: Cavendish Torsion Balance
visualization.purpose: Explain how the tiny gravitational interaction can be measured.
visualization.note: Interactive component not yet built. Controls and outputs below define exactly what the next AI-generated visualizer for this topic should let the student manipulate and see.

key_points: Do not confuse G with g.
common_mistakes: Writing the wrong power of length in dimensions.
Treating G as dependent on distance.
Do not confuse G with g.
neet_tips: Memorize both SI unit and dimensions of G.

introduction.summary: Acceleration due to gravity is the acceleration of a freely falling body caused by the gravitational attraction of a celestial body.

explanation: Acceleration due to gravity is the acceleration of a freely falling body caused by the gravitational attraction of a celestial body.
Near Earth's surface, g is approximately 9.8 m/s^2.
Ignoring air resistance, g is independent of the mass of the falling object.

explanation.heading: Conclusions
points: g depends on the mass and radius of the planet.
g is not the same everywhere on Earth.

worked_example.title: Surface g
worked_example.problem: Express g in terms of G, Earth mass M and radius R.
worked_example.solution: Equate GMm/R² with mg and cancel m.

worked_example.title: Mass independence
worked_example.problem: Two objects of different masses fall without air resistance. Which has larger g?
worked_example.solution: The object mass cancels from the derivation of g.
worked_example.answer: Both have the same g at the same location.

worked_example.title: Planet scaling
worked_example.problem: A planet has twice Earth’s mass and the same radius. Compare surface g.
worked_example.solution: g∝M/R², so g′=2g.

visualization.title: Free Fall on Different Worlds
visualization.purpose: Show that g depends on the attracting body, not the falling object mass.
visualization.note: Interactive component not yet built. Controls and outputs below define exactly what the next AI-generated visualizer for this topic should let the student manipulate and see.

key_points: Ignoring air resistance, g is independent of falling mass.
g depends on the mass and radius of the attracting body.
common_mistakes: Using the falling object mass in the final formula for g.
Assuming g is identical everywhere on Earth.
neet_tips: Use g=GM/R² and cancel the test mass immediately.

introduction.summary: Mass measures inertia; weight is gravitational force and therefore changes when local g changes.

explanation: Mass - kg - Measure of inertia - False
Weight - N - Gravitational force acting on an object - True
g - m/s^2 - Acceleration due to gravity - True

explanation.heading: Moon
points: Mass remains unchanged on the Moon.
Weight changes because lunar g is smaller.
Weight on Moon is approximately one-sixth of weight on Earth.

worked_example.title: Moon weight
worked_example.problem: An object has mass m on Earth. What happens to its mass on the Moon?
worked_example.solution: Mass is intrinsic and remains m; weight becomes mg_moon.

worked_example.title: Weight ratio
worked_example.problem: If local g becomes half, what happens to weight?
worked_example.solution: W=mg and m is unchanged, so W′=W/2.

worked_example.title: Mass reading
worked_example.problem: Can a beam balance measuring mass change its mass reading merely by moving to the Moon?
worked_example.solution: Mass does not depend on local g.

visualization.title: Visit Different Planets
visualization.note: Interactive component not yet built. Controls and outputs below define exactly what the next AI-generated visualizer for this topic should let the student manipulate and see.

key_points: Moon weight is approximately one-sixth of Earth weight.
common_mistakes: Reporting weight in kilograms as if kg were a force unit.
Changing mass when only g changes.

topics.title: Variation of g with Altitude and Depth

introduction.summary: The value of g changes with position relative to Earth’s surface.

points.conclusion: g decreases linearly with depth and becomes zero at the centre.

worked_example.title: Altitude ratio
worked_example.problem: At h=R, compare g_h with surface g.

worked_example.title: Small height
worked_example.problem: For h≪R, what fractional decrease occurs?
worked_example.solution: From g_h≈g(1−2h/R), fractional decrease is 2h/R.

worked_example.title: Small depth
worked_example.problem: For depth d in a uniform-density Earth, what fractional decrease occurs?

visualization.title: Move Above and Below Earth
visualization.purpose: Show different altitude and depth laws on the same Earth model.
visualization.note: Interactive component not yet built. Controls and outputs below define exactly what the next AI-generated visualizer for this topic should let the student manipulate and see.

key_points: Depth: linear decrease for uniform density.
At Earth centre g=0 in the ideal model.
common_mistakes: Using 1−h/R for small altitude.
Using the depth formula for altitude.
Forgetting r=R+h is measured from Earth centre.
Do not use the altitude formula for depth.
At Earth's centre, g = 0 in the ideal symmetric model, but gravitational potential is not zero.
neet_tips: Remember: small height gives factor 2; small depth gives factor 1.

introduction.summary: Gravitational field describes the gravitational influence around a mass and is measured as force per unit test mass.

explanation: A gravitational field is the region around a mass in which another mass experiences gravitational force.
Field strength is gravitational force per unit test mass.
The field due to an isolated point mass points toward the source mass.

worked_example.title: Field strength
worked_example.problem: A 15 kg body experiences 45 N gravitational force. Find field strength.
worked_example.solution: g_field=F/m=45/15.

worked_example.title: Direction
worked_example.problem: What is the field direction due to an isolated mass?
worked_example.solution: Gravitational attraction points toward the source mass.

worked_example.title: Neutral point
worked_example.problem: Can the net field be zero while potential is nonzero?
worked_example.solution: Yes. Vector fields can cancel while scalar potentials add.

visualization.title: Gravitational Field Lines and Vectors
visualization.purpose: Show vector addition and neutral points.
visualization.note: Interactive component not yet built. Controls and outputs below define exactly what the next AI-generated visualizer for this topic should let the student manipulate and see.

key_points: Field magnitude from a point mass follows inverse-square dependence.
common_mistakes: Treating field like scalar potential.
Ignoring direction in superposition.
neet_tips: For zero field between unequal masses, set magnitudes equal and choose the point between them.

introduction.summary: Gravitational potential energy describes the energy associated with the configuration of masses.

explanation: Gravitational potential energy is the energy associated with the position of a mass in a gravitational field.
Taking potential energy to be zero at infinity, the gravitational potential energy of mass m at distance r from point mass M is negative.
The negative sign indicates a bound gravitational state relative to infinity.

explanation.heading: Near Surface
points: For small changes in height near Earth's surface, ΔU ≈ mgh.

explanation.heading: Important
points: Use U = -GMm/r for large-scale planetary problems.
Choice of zero potential energy is a reference convention.

worked_example.title: Energy change to 2R
worked_example.problem: Raise mass m from R to 3R from Earth’s centre. Find ΔU.
worked_example.solution: ΔU=GMm(1/R−1/3R)=2GMm/(3R)=2mgR/3.

worked_example.title: Sign
worked_example.problem: Why is U negative when zero is at infinity?
worked_example.solution: A bound configuration has lower energy than infinite separation.

worked_example.title: Near surface
worked_example.problem: When is mgh acceptable?
worked_example.solution: For small changes in height compared with Earth’s radius, g is approximately constant.
worked_example.answer: Near Earth’s surface for small h.

visualization.title: Energy vs Distance
visualization.purpose: Show negative bound energy and its approach to zero at infinity.
visualization.note: Interactive component not yet built. Controls and outputs below define exactly what the next AI-generated visualizer for this topic should let the student manipulate and see.

common_mistakes: Using mgh for huge heights without checking.
Forgetting the negative sign in U.
neet_tips: For large heights, calculate ΔU using the difference of −GMm/r values.

introduction.summary: Gravitational potential is the potential energy per unit mass at a point.

explanation: Gravitational potential at a point is gravitational potential energy per unit mass.
It is a scalar quantity.
With zero potential at infinity, the potential due to a point mass is negative.

formulae.label: Gravitational Potential
formulae.formula: For several source masses: V_total = Σ(-GMi/ri)

worked_example.title: Potential at height
worked_example.problem: If surface potential is V0=−GM/R, find potential at r=2R.

worked_example.title: Zero field versus potential
worked_example.problem: At a neutral point, must potential be zero?
worked_example.solution: No. Field is a vector and can cancel; potential is scalar and can remain nonzero.

worked_example.title: Multiple sources
worked_example.problem: How are potentials from several masses combined?
worked_example.solution: Add them algebraically because potential is scalar.

visualization.title: Gravitational Potential Landscape
visualization.purpose: Show why potential is scalar and negative with zero at infinity.
visualization.note: Interactive component not yet built. Controls and outputs below define exactly what the next AI-generated visualizer for this topic should let the student manipulate and see.

key_points: V=−GM/r for a point mass with zero at infinity.
Zero field does not imply zero potential.
common_mistakes: Adding potential vectors.
Confusing potential V with potential energy U.
Potential is scalar, gravitational field is vector.
Zero field does not necessarily mean zero potential.
At Earth's centre the field is zero in the ideal symmetric model, while potential remains finite and negative.
neet_tips: For several masses, add V values directly with signs.

introduction.summary: Escape speed is the minimum launch speed needed to reach infinity with zero final speed under the ideal assumptions.

explanation: Escape speed is the minimum speed required at the surface of a celestial body for an object to reach infinity with zero final speed, neglecting atmosphere and other bodies.
derivation: At infinity for minimum escape condition, kinetic energy = 0 and potential energy = 0.
Conservation of energy gives 1/2 m v_e^2 = GMm/R.

worked_example.title: Earth escape speed
worked_example.problem: Using g≈9.8 m/s² and R≈6.4×10^6 m, estimate escape speed.
worked_example.solution: v_e=√(2gR), giving approximately 11.2 km/s.

worked_example.title: Mass independence
worked_example.problem: Does doubling the projectile mass double escape speed?
worked_example.solution: No; projectile mass cancels from the energy equation.

worked_example.title: Relation to orbital speed
worked_example.problem: Compare escape and circular orbital speed at the same radius.
worked_example.solution: v_e=√2 v_o.
worked_example.answer: Escape speed is √2 times orbital speed.

visualization.title: Escape Speed (vₑ) Launch Simulation
visualization.description: Student sets a launch speed and fires a projectile from Earth's surface. Below vₑ ≈ 11.2 km/s it rises and falls back; at or above vₑ it escapes off-screen — turning the abstract inequality v0 >= ve into something they watch happen.

key_points: Greater than circular orbital speed by √2 at same radius.
Escape speed is independent of projectile mass.
For Earth it is approximately 11.2 km/s.
Escape speed is greater than circular orbital speed at the same radius by a factor of sqrt(2).
common_mistakes: Using v_e=√(GM/R) instead of √(2GM/R).
Confusing escape speed with orbital speed.
Do not confuse escape speed with orbital speed.
The projectile mass cancels.
neet_tips: Use ratios v_e∝√(M/R) for planet-comparison questions.

introduction.summary: An Earth satellite remains in orbit because gravitational attraction supplies the required centripetal acceleration.

explanation: A satellite is a body revolving around a larger body under gravitational influence.
For a circular orbit, gravity provides the centripetal acceleration.
A satellite can remain in an ideal orbit without continuous propulsion because its tangential motion and gravitational acceleration combine to produce curved motion.

formulae.label: Earth Satellites and Orbital Motion
formulae.formula: At Earth's surface: v_o = sqrt(GM/R) = sqrt(gR)

worked_example.title: Orbital speed ratio
worked_example.problem: If orbital radius becomes 4R, how does speed change?

worked_example.title: Period ratio
worked_example.problem: If orbital radius becomes 4R, how does period change?

worked_example.title: Tangential motion
worked_example.problem: If gravity suddenly disappeared, what happens to the satellite’s instantaneous velocity?
worked_example.solution: With no force, velocity remains unchanged in magnitude and direction at that instant, so it moves tangentially.
worked_example.answer: Continues tangentially with same instantaneous speed.

visualization.title: Earth Satellite Orbital Motion Simulator
visualization.description: A slider sets orbital altitude h from 400 km to 20,000 km; the canvas animates the satellite's orbit while orbital speed vo = sqrt(GM/r) and time period T update live, showing that higher orbits are slower and take longer.

key_points: Satellite mass cancels from orbital speed.
common_mistakes: Using r=h instead of r=R+h.
Thinking constant speed means zero acceleration.
Orbital velocity decreases as r increases.
Satellite mass cancels from orbital velocity.
A circularly orbiting satellite is accelerating even if its speed is constant.
neet_tips: For satellite ratios, use v∝r^-1/2 and T∝r^3/2.

introduction.summary: Geostationary satellites appear fixed over one point on Earth because their orbital motion matches Earth’s rotation.

explanation: A geostationary satellite appears fixed relative to a point on Earth's surface.

explanation.heading: Conditions
points: Orbit lies in Earth's equatorial plane.
Moves west to east, the direction of Earth's rotation.
Orbital period equals Earth's rotational period.
Its angular speed matches Earth's rotation.

worked_example.title: Necessary conditions
worked_example.problem: Is a 24-hour period alone sufficient for geostationary status?
worked_example.solution: No. Circular equatorial orbit and correct direction are also required.

worked_example.title: Direction
worked_example.problem: Which direction must a geostationary satellite move?
worked_example.solution: It must move west to east, the same sense as Earth’s rotation.

worked_example.title: Use
worked_example.problem: Why are geostationary satellites useful for communication?
worked_example.solution: They appear fixed over a region, allowing fixed ground antennas to point toward them.

visualization.title: Geostationary vs. Polar Satellites Comparison
visualization.description: A toggle switches the diagram between an equatorial geostationary orbit and a pole-to-pole polar orbit, with a side-by-side card comparing period, altitude and typical use for each.

common_mistakes: Calling every 24-hour satellite geostationary.
Putting the orbit in a polar plane.
A 24-hour period alone is not sufficient; the equatorial plane, circular orbit and correct direction are also required.
neet_tips: Use the four-condition checklist in every geostationary question.

introduction.summary: A circular satellite has positive kinetic energy, negative potential energy and negative total mechanical energy.

explanation: For a circular orbit, kinetic energy is positive and gravitational potential energy is negative.
Total mechanical energy is negative, showing that the satellite is gravitationally bound.
When a satellite is moved to a higher circular orbit, orbital speed and kinetic energy decrease, while potential energy and total mechanical energy increase (become less negative).

worked_example.title: Energy relation
worked_example.problem: If K=5 J for a circular satellite, find U and E.
worked_example.solution: U=−2K and E=−K.

worked_example.title: Higher orbit
worked_example.problem: What happens to K when r increases?
worked_example.solution: K∝1/r, so K decreases.

worked_example.title: Binding energy
worked_example.problem: What is the magnitude of energy needed to remove a circular satellite to infinity?
worked_example.solution: It equals |E|=GMm/(2r).

visualization.title: Satellite Energy Balance
visualization.purpose: Show how K, U and E change with orbit size.
visualization.note: Interactive component not yet built. Controls and outputs below define exactly what the next AI-generated visualizer for this topic should let the student manipulate and see.

key_points: Higher orbit means less negative total energy.
common_mistakes: Calling negative total energy positive binding energy.
Assuming U becomes more negative at larger r.
neet_tips: Memorize U=−2K and E=−K for circular orbits.

introduction.summary: Spherical symmetry simplifies gravitational calculations and explains shell results, centre behaviour and superposition.

explanation: Outside a spherically symmetric body, its gravitational effect can be treated as though its entire mass were concentrated at its centre.
For an ideal spherical shell, gravitational field inside the shell is zero.
For a uniform solid sphere, gravitational field inside varies linearly with distance from the centre.

formulae.label: Spherically Symmetric Bodies
formulae.formula: Inside uniform sphere: g(r) = GMr/R^3 = g_surface(r/R)

worked_example.title: Shell interior
worked_example.problem: What is gravitational field inside an ideal spherical shell?
worked_example.solution: Contributions cancel by spherical symmetry.

worked_example.title: Uniform sphere centre
worked_example.problem: What is g at the centre of a uniform solid sphere?
worked_example.solution: g(r)∝r inside, so at r=0, g=0.

worked_example.title: Outside body
worked_example.problem: Can a spherically symmetric body be treated as a point mass outside it?
worked_example.solution: Yes, with the whole mass concentrated at its centre for the external gravitational effect.

visualization.title: Inside and Outside a Spherical Body
visualization.purpose: Compare shell, solid sphere and external field.
visualization.note: Interactive component not yet built. Controls and outputs below define exactly what the next AI-generated visualizer for this topic should let the student manipulate and see.

key_points: Uniform solid sphere interior field is proportional to r.
Zero field does not imply zero potential.
common_mistakes: Using GM/r² inside a shell.
Assuming potential is zero whenever field is zero.
Zero gravitational field at a point does not imply zero gravitational potential at that point.
neet_tips: First identify whether the point is inside, on, or outside the spherical body.

traps.claim: Doubling the mass of a falling object doubles g.
traps.why: The object's mass cancels from GMm/R^2 = mg.

traps.claim: G and g are the same quantity.
traps.why: G is universal gravitational constant; g is acceleration due to gravity.
Potential is scalar; field is vector.

traps.claim: At Earth's centre both g and gravitational potential are zero.
traps.why: g is zero in the ideal symmetric model, but potential is finite and negative when zero is chosen at infinity.

traps.claim: Escape velocity depends on projectile mass.
traps.why: Projectile mass cancels in the energy equation.

traps.claim: Satellite speed increases when orbital radius increases.
traps.why: v_o = sqrt(GM/r), so it decreases with r.

traps.claim: Any satellite with a 24-hour period is geostationary.
traps.why: It must also be circular, equatorial and rotate west-to-east with Earth.

reference_pages.title: NEET Problem-Solving Strategy
steps: Identify the required quantity: force, g, potential, energy, escape speed, orbital speed, period or satellite energy.
Check whether distance is measured from Earth's centre or surface.
Use r = R+h for a satellite at height h.
Convert to SI units when required.
For ratio questions, use proportionality before calculating.
Use energy conservation for escape speed and orbital energy.
Use gravitational force = centripetal force for circular satellite motion.
Finally compare the answer with the physical expectation.

reference_pages.title: One-Minute Revision
points: Kepler 1: elliptical orbit, Sun at one focus.
Kepler 2: equal areas in equal times.
g decreases with depth and is zero at Earth's centre in the ideal uniform-density model.
Geostationary satellite: equatorial, circular, west-to-east, same rotational period as Earth.

Ideal escape speed from Earth's surface
Ideal circular orbital speed close to Earth's surface
